Generate an ML-KEM key pair

Source: R/kem.R
kemkg.Rd

Generates a key pair for ML-KEM (FIPS 203), the standardised post-quantum key encapsulation mechanism, and kempubkey() strips a key pair down to the half that can be shared. Use them when a capsule, a data file or a credential has to reach one recipient without being readable on the way: the recipient makes the key pair and publishes the public half, and the sender uses it with kemencap(). It is implemented in this package, with no system dependency.

Usage

kemkg(lvl = 768L, seed = NULL)

kempubkey(key)

Arguments

lvl

Security level, one whole number: 512 (ML-KEM-512, NIST category 1), 768 (the default, category 3) or 1024 (category 5). 768 is the level NIST and the IETF have settled on for general use.

seed

Optional raw vector of 64 seed bytes ( d || z) . Supplying it makes the key reproducible, which is what the standard's test vectors need; the default draws from the operating system's CSPRNG.

key

For kempubkey(): a key pair from kemkg().

Value

kemkg(): a list of class c("bricklayer_kem_key", "list") with public (character, the encapsulation key as lower-case hex, 800, 1184 or 1568 bytes), secret (character, the decapsulation key as hex, 1632, 2400 or 3168 bytes) and level (integer). Printing it never shows the secret. kempubkey(): a list of class c("bricklayer_kem_public_key", "list") with public and level only.

Details

A KEM is not a signature scheme and not a cipher. Encapsulation produces two things: a ciphertext to send, and a 32-byte shared secret to keep. The holder of the decapsulation key recovers the same secret from the ciphertext. What either side then does with that secret – feed it to a KDF, key an AEAD – is outside the mechanism.

Key generation is ML-KEM.KeyGen of FIPS 203 (Algorithm 19) from the 64-byte seed \(d \| z\): \(d\) seeds the K-PKE key and \(z\) is the implicit-rejection value kept inside the decapsulation key. With a seed the result is deterministic (the same seed gives the same key, which is how the NIST test vectors are reproduced); without one the seed is drawn with rndbytes() from the operating system. The key sizes per level are given by kemsz(); the level is not recorded in a ciphertext, so both sides must agree on it.

Errors: lvl other than one whole number 512, 768 or 1024; seed that is not a raw vector of 64 bytes; key passed to kempubkey() that is not from kemkg().

Security

The implementation is hand-written. Its standardised schemes are checked byte for byte against OpenSSL 3.5 and NIST known-answer vectors in the test suite. Side channels are checked, not assumed: inst/ctcheck runs every operation that touches a secret under valgrind memcheck with the secret marked undefined (the ctgrind method), so a branch or a memory address that depends on it is a reported error, and afterwards scans the dead stack for copies of the secret. Both checks run in CI on every change, with GCC and with Clang. Timing is also measured on x86-64 and arm64 hardware (inst/dudect), power leakage is assessed in simulation under the value and the transition models (inst/tvla), and ML-KEM decapsulation and ML-DSA signing are first-order masked by default. These are checks of this code on those compilers and under those leakage models; the README's security section lists what each check does and does not cover.

References

National Institute of Standards and Technology (2024). Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard. FIPS 203. doi:10.6028/NIST.FIPS.203

See also

kemencap(), kemdecap(), kemsz(), fipskg() for the signature schemes.

Examples

key <- kemkg(768)
pub <- kempubkey(key)

# the sender holds only the public key
sent <- kemencap(pub)
# the recipient recovers the same secret from the ciphertext
got <- kemdecap(key, sent$ciphertext)
identical(sent$shared, got)
#> [1] TRUE

# a corrupted ciphertext yields a DIFFERENT secret, not an error
bad <- sent$ciphertext
substring(bad, 1L, 2L) <- "00"
identical(kemdecap(key, bad), got)
#> [1] FALSE

# a fixed seed gives the same key every time (for test vectors only)
k1 <- kemkg(512, seed = as.raw(0:63))
k2 <- kemkg(512, seed = as.raw(0:63))
identical(k1$public, k2$public)
#> [1] TRUE
k1
#> ── Key encapsulation key (ML-KEM, FIPS 203) ──────────────────────
#>   level       ML-KEM-512
#>   public key  3995815e597d104355cf29aa5333c932... (800 bytes)
#>   secret      <withheld>
#> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# levels other than the three FIPS 203 defines are refused
try(kemkg(256))
#> Error : `level` must be one of 512, 768 or 1024
try(kemkg(768, seed = as.raw(1:10)))
#> Error : `seed` must be a raw vector of 64 bytes
